# Speech Representation Learning and Foundation Models {#sec-ssl}

The previous chapter ended with an economic problem. End-to-end ASR works, but
it wants thousands of hours of transcribed audio per language, and transcription
is expensive, slow, and requires literate speakers of the target language. There
are roughly 7,000 living languages. Fewer than a hundred have the labelled
corpora that @sec-e2e assumes.

Unlabelled speech, by contrast, is nearly free. Radio archives, podcasts,
parliamentary recordings, and video platforms supply orders of magnitude more
audio than anyone has ever transcribed. **Self-supervised learning** is the
attempt to convert that abundance into a usable prior: pre-train an encoder on
raw audio with an objective that requires no transcripts, then fine-tune it on
whatever small labelled set exists.

This chapter is about how that is done, what the resulting representations
actually contain, and how they are evaluated. It is shorter than the last
chapter because the *conceptual* content is smaller — essentially one idea with
three implementations — but its reach is larger. The encoders described here are
the front-end of nearly every system in the rest of this book: the speaker
embeddings of @sec-features, the semantic tokens of @sec-semantic-acoustic, the
emotion and audio-captioning models of @sec-paralinguistics, and the audio inputs of speech
language models all begin with a network trained by one of these objectives.

::: {.callout-note}
## The one-sentence summary

The recipe that won is **masked prediction of discrete units**, and the three
families in this chapter are three different answers to the question *where do
the discrete targets come from?*
:::


## Why Self-Supervision Is Hard for Speech {#sec-ssl-design}

Self-supervision means inventing a *pretext task*: a supervised problem whose
labels are derived from the input itself. In text this is easy, because language
arrives pre-discretised. BERT masks a token and asks which of 30,000 vocabulary
items it was; the answer is a well-defined categorical variable, cross-entropy
applies, and the model is forced to learn syntax and semantics to succeed.

Speech has no vocabulary. The signal is continuous, high-rate, and — this is the
crux — **locally very predictable for uninteresting reasons**. Given the
waveform up to time $t$, the sample at $t+1$ is almost determined by the local
waveform's smoothness. A model trained to regress the next sample, or the next
spectrogram frame, under an $L_2$ loss will spend nearly all of its capacity on
low-level detail: signal continuity, channel colouration, background noise
level, speaker timbre. None of that is what a downstream task needs.

Three design problems follow, and every model in this chapter is positioned by
how it answers them.

1. **What is the prediction target?** Regressing the raw signal invites the
   failure above. The alternative is to predict something *quantised* — to force
   the model to commit to categorical, phone-like distinctions rather than
   hedging with a conditional mean. This is the central insight of the field.
2. **Where does the quantisation come from?** There is no ground-truth phone
   inventory. The targets must be discovered, and the discovery is circular:
   good units require a good model, and a good model requires good units.
3. **What is masked, and at what granularity?** Speech is redundant over short
   windows. Masking a single 20 ms frame is trivially solvable by interpolation,
   so useful pretext tasks mask *spans* long enough that local smoothness is not
   enough.

@tbl-ssl-timeline places the main answers in order.

| Year | Model | Family | Key idea |
|:-----|:------|:-------|:---------|
| 2018 | CPC [@oord2018cpc] | Contrastive | Predict the future in *latent* space with InfoNCE |
| 2019 | APC [@chung2019apc] | Predictive | Autoregressive prediction of future spectrogram frames |
| 2019 | wav2vec [@schneider2019wav2vec] | Contrastive | CPC applied to ASR; features replace log-Mel |
| 2019 | vq-wav2vec [@baevski2020vqwav2vec] | Contrastive + VQ | Discretise audio, then run a plain BERT on the tokens |
| 2020 | **wav2vec 2.0** [@baevski2020wav2vec2] | Contrastive + VQ | Mask spans, contrast against *jointly learned* quantised targets |
| 2021 | **HuBERT** [@hsu2021hubert] | Masked prediction | Offline $k$-means targets, refined iteratively |
| 2021 | w2v-BERT [@chung2021w2vbert] | Hybrid | Contrastive module learns the inventory, MLM module models context |
| 2021 | **WavLM** [@chen2022wavlm] | Masked prediction | HuBERT plus simulated noise and overlap; denoising |
| 2022 | data2vec [@baevski2022data2vec] | Self-distillation | Regress *contextualised* targets from an EMA teacher |
| 2022 | **BEST-RQ** [@chiu2022bestrq] | Random projection | Frozen random codebook; no learned quantiser at all |

: Timeline of self-supervised speech models. {#tbl-ssl-timeline}


## Contrastive Objectives {#sec-contrastive}

### Contrastive Predictive Coding {#sec-cpc}

CPC [@oord2018cpc] is the ancestor. Its move is to abandon reconstruction
entirely: rather than predicting the future *signal*, predict the future
*latent*, and score the prediction by discrimination rather than regression.

An encoder $f$ maps the input to latents $\mathbf{z}_t = f(\mathbf{x}_t)$, and an
autoregressive network $g$ summarises the past into a context
$\mathbf{c}_t = g(\mathbf{z}_{\leq t})$. For each offset $k$, a bilinear scorer
must pick the true future latent $\mathbf{z}_{t+k}$ out of a set $\mathcal{Z}$
containing one positive and $N-1$ negatives sampled from elsewhere:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}
= -\,\mathbb{E}\left[\log \frac{\exp\!\big(\mathbf{z}_{t+k}^{\top} \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{c}_t\big)}
{\sum_{\tilde{\mathbf{z}} \in \mathcal{Z}} \exp\!\big(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{\top} \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{c}_t\big)}\right]
$$ {#eq-infonce}

Two properties make this the right shape for speech. First, it is a **variational
lower bound on mutual information**: minimising @eq-infonce maximises a bound
$I(\mathbf{z}_{t+k}; \mathbf{c}_t) \geq \log N - \mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}$,
so the context is pushed to retain exactly the information that is predictive of
the future and free to discard everything else. Second, discrimination against
negatives sidesteps the conditional-mean problem: there is no averaging, because
the model never has to *produce* a signal, only to rank candidates.

**wav2vec** [@schneider2019wav2vec] applied this to ASR directly — a fully
convolutional encoder and context network trained with a CPC-style loss on
unlabelled audio, whose output replaces log-Mel features as the input to an
acoustic model. It was the first clear demonstration that self-supervised
pre-training *reduces WER* on standard benchmarks, which converted SSL from a
representation-learning curiosity into a speech method.

**vq-wav2vec** [@baevski2020vqwav2vec] is the pivotal intermediate step and the
best teaching device in this section. It inserts a vector quantiser so that
audio becomes a sequence of *discrete tokens*, which can then be fed to an
off-the-shelf BERT. Two consequences follow, one immediate and one that took
three years to pay off: the two-stage pipeline worked well, and — more
importantly — it established that speech could be treated as a sequence of
symbols drawn from a learned vocabulary. Every discrete-token model in this
book, including the neural audio codecs and the speech language models, descends
from that framing.

### wav2vec 2.0 {#sec-wav2vec2}

wav2vec 2.0 [@baevski2020wav2vec2] collapses vq-wav2vec's two stages into one
jointly-trained model and is, by influence, the most important paper in this
chapter.

The architecture has three parts. A **feature encoder** — a seven-layer temporal
CNN with 20 ms stride — maps the raw waveform to latents $\mathbf{z}_t$. A
**context network**, a Transformer, maps the (partially masked) latent sequence
to contextualised representations $\mathbf{c}_t$. And a **quantiser** maps each
*unmasked* latent to a discrete code $\mathbf{q}_t$, which serves as the
prediction target.

Spans are masked in the latent sequence: a proportion of time steps are sampled
as start indices and the following $M \approx 10$ steps (200 ms) are replaced
with a learned mask embedding. The model must then identify the true quantised
latent at each masked position, against distractors sampled from other masked
positions in the same utterance:

$$
\mathcal{L}_m = -\log \frac{\exp\!\big(\text{sim}(\mathbf{c}_t, \mathbf{q}_t)/\kappa\big)}
{\sum_{\tilde{\mathbf{q}} \sim \mathbf{Q}_t} \exp\!\big(\text{sim}(\mathbf{c}_t, \tilde{\mathbf{q}})/\kappa\big)}
$$ {#eq-w2v2-contrastive}

with $\text{sim}$ the cosine similarity and $\kappa$ a temperature.

**Product quantisation and the Gumbel trick.** The quantiser uses $G$ codebooks
of $V$ entries each; a latent is mapped to one entry per codebook and the $G$
selections are concatenated and projected, giving $V^G$ effective targets from
only $GV$ parameters (in the original, $G = 2$, $V = 320$, hence 102,400
possible targets). Selection is a discrete $\arg\max$, which has no gradient, so
training uses the Gumbel-softmax with a straight-through estimator: the forward
pass takes the hard $\arg\max$, the backward pass uses

$$
p_{g,v} = \frac{\exp\big((l_{g,v} + n_v)/\tau\big)}{\sum_{k=1}^{V} \exp\big((l_{g,k} + n_k)/\tau\big)},
\qquad n_v = -\log(-\log u_v), \; u_v \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)
$$ {#eq-gumbel}

with the temperature $\tau$ annealed from 2 to 0.5 over training, moving the
relaxation gradually toward the hard discrete behaviour it approximates.

**Codebook collapse and the diversity loss.** Left alone, a learned quantiser
degenerates: a handful of entries absorb all the probability mass, the effective
vocabulary shrinks, and the contrastive task becomes trivial because the
distractors are usually the same code as the positive. The fix is an auxiliary
term that maximises the entropy of *average* codebook usage across a batch,

$$
\mathcal{L}_d = \frac{1}{GV}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\Big(-H(\bar{p}_g)\Big)
= \frac{1}{GV}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{v=1}^{V} \bar{p}_{g,v} \log \bar{p}_{g,v}
$$ {#eq-diversity}

where $\bar{p}_{g,v}$ is the mean softmax probability of entry $v$ in codebook
$g$ over the batch. The total objective is
$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_m + \alpha \mathcal{L}_d$. Codebook collapse recurs
throughout this book — it is the same failure that afflicts the neural audio
codecs of @sec-collapse — and @eq-diversity is the first of several answers to
it.

**Why it mattered.** The headline result reframed the economics of ASR:
competitive word error rates from **ten minutes** of labelled speech, and
4.8/8.2% on LibriSpeech `test-clean`/`test-other` using only that, after
pre-training on the 53k unlabelled hours of Libri-Light [@kahn2020librilight].
Fine-tuning is simply a CTC head (@sec-ctc) on top of the context network. For
the thousands of languages with no transcribed corpora, this was the unlock, and
it is the reason the multilingual programme of @sec-multilingual became
thinkable.


## Masked Prediction with Learned Targets {#sec-masked-pred}

### HuBERT {#sec-hubert}

wav2vec 2.0 trains the quantiser and the context model against each other, which
works but is delicate — the target distribution moves while it is being
predicted. HuBERT [@hsu2021hubert] sidesteps the instability with a
deliberately low-tech alternative: **compute the targets offline, then treat the
problem as ordinary masked classification.**

The procedure is a loop:

1. Run $k$-means on 39-dimensional MFCCs of the training audio. The resulting
   cluster assignments $z_t \in \{1, \ldots, C\}$ are noisy pseudo-labels — but
   they are *categorical*, which is all the objective needs.
2. Mask spans of the input and train a Transformer to predict the cluster label
   at masked positions, with a cross-entropy over a learned code embedding
   $\mathbf{e}_c$:

$$
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{t \in M} \log p(z_t \mid \tilde{\mathbf{X}}, t),
\qquad
p(c \mid \tilde{\mathbf{X}}, t) = \frac{\exp\big(\text{sim}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{e}_c)/\tau\big)}
{\sum_{c'=1}^{C} \exp\big(\text{sim}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{e}_{c'})/\tau\big)}
$$ {#eq-hubert}

where $\mathbf{o}_t$ is the Transformer output, $\mathbf{A}$ a projection, and
$M$ the masked index set.
3. Re-run $k$-means, now on the *hidden representations of the model just
   trained*, to obtain better labels. Return to step 2.

**Two details carry most of the weight.** First, the loss is computed **only at
masked positions**. Scoring unmasked frames as well lets the model solve the
task by copying the local input through, which is exactly the trivial solution
of @sec-ssl-design; restricting to masked spans forces it to use context. This
single choice is worth a large accuracy difference and is the clearest
demonstration in the chapter that *what you do not train on* matters as much as
what you do.

Second, the iterative refinement genuinely bootstraps. MFCC clusters are barely
better than chance at separating phones. But a model trained to predict them
must learn contextual structure to do so, and its hidden layers therefore
organise phonetically; clustering *those* yields substantially cleaner units,
and the next iteration is better again. Measured phone purity climbs at each
round. The circularity identified in @sec-ssl-design is resolved not by solving
it but by iterating through it — the same trick as the forced-alignment loop of
the classical ASR pipeline, and worth pointing out as such.

HuBERT's discrete units became the field's default "semantic tokens", and that
is arguably its largest downstream consequence. When @sec-semantic-acoustic
describes a codec whose first residual codebook is distilled to match WavLM
features, or a speech language model operating over discrete units, the lineage
runs through @eq-hubert.

### WavLM {#sec-wavlm}

WavLM [@chen2022wavlm] keeps HuBERT's objective and changes the *data*. During
pre-training, utterances are augmented by mixing in noise and — crucially —
**overlapping speech from other utterances**, while the prediction target
remains the units of the *original* clean primary speaker. The masked-prediction
task therefore becomes a masked *denoising* task: the model must reconstruct
what the target speaker said while ignoring an interfering one.

The consequences are exactly what that objective would predict. WavLM is the
strongest general-purpose speech encoder of its generation on tasks that require
holding onto speaker identity under adverse conditions: speaker verification,
diarization (@sec-features), and separation. Its lesson generalises well beyond
speech — **robustness is a property you train for, not a property you bolt on**
— and it explains why WavLM, rather than a newer or larger model, is still the
standard backbone for speaker similarity scoring, including the speaker
similarity metric used to evaluate zero-shot speech synthesis (@sec-tts-objective).

### data2vec {#sec-data2vec}

data2vec [@baevski2022data2vec] asks whether the targets need to be discrete at
all. It replaces them with **contextualised latent targets produced by an
exponential-moving-average teacher** — the same network, at a lagged parameter
average:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{t \in M} \big\| f_\theta(\tilde{\mathbf{X}})_t - \mathbf{y}_t \big\|^2,
\qquad
\mathbf{y}_t = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{l = L-K+1}^{L} \hat{\mathbf{a}}_t^{(l)},
\qquad
\Delta \leftarrow \tau\Delta + (1-\tau)\theta
$$ {#eq-data2vec}

where $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_t^{(l)}$ are normalised activations of the teacher's top
$K$ layers and $\Delta$ are the teacher parameters. Because the teacher sees the
*unmasked* input, its representation at a masked position is contextual rather
than local, which avoids the trivial-solution problem without needing
quantisation.

Its significance is partly methodological: the identical algorithm, with only
the input encoder changed, works for speech, vision, and text. It is the
modality-agnostic pole of the design space, and a useful counterweight to the
claim that discretisation is essential.


## Random-Projection Quantisation {#sec-rpq}

The last family is the simplest and, measured by citations alone, the most
underrated in this chapter.

BEST-RQ [@chiu2022bestrq] observes that if the point of quantisation is merely
to produce *consistent categorical targets*, the quantiser does not have to be
learned, or even good. It uses a projection matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and a codebook
$\mathbf{C} = [\mathbf{c}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{c}_V]$ that are **randomly
initialised and then frozen forever**:

$$
y_t = \arg\min_{v \in \{1,\ldots,V\}} \big\| \, \text{norm}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_t) - \mathbf{c}_v \, \big\|_2
$$ {#eq-bestrq}

with training a plain cross-entropy on masked positions against these labels.
There is no codebook learning, no diversity loss, no clustering loop, no EMA
teacher, and no moving target.

That this works at all is the interesting part, and the reason is worth stating.
A random projection is, with high probability, approximately distance-preserving
(the Johnson–Lindenstrauss property), so acoustically similar frames land near
each other in the projected space and therefore receive the same label.
The labels are not *phonetic*, but they are *consistent*: the same sound gets
the same symbol. Consistency, it turns out, is the only property the
masked-prediction objective actually requires — the phonetic organisation is
something the model builds for itself in order to predict those labels from
context.

**Why it is under-cited relative to its influence.** BEST-RQ was adopted
primarily inside industry rather than reproduced in academia. It is the
pre-training objective of Google's USM [@zhang2023usm] and hence of production
ASR across 100+ languages, and it has propagated into subsequent large-scale
audio systems. Its citation count sits an order of magnitude below wav2vec 2.0's
while its deployed footprint is comparable. It belongs in any teaching treatment
as the **third canonical objective**, alongside contrastive learning and
offline-cluster masked prediction.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading citation counts

BEST-RQ is a good calibration case for the impact heuristics used elsewhere in
this book. Papers whose contribution ships inside a product rather than a
checkpoint are systematically under-cited, because the citations accrue to the
system, not the method. Treat a low count on an industrial-lab paper as weak
evidence, not as a verdict.
:::

### Comparing the Families {#sec-ssl-compare}

| | **Contrastive** (wav2vec 2.0) | **Offline cluster** (HuBERT, WavLM) | **Random projection** (BEST-RQ) | **Self-distillation** (data2vec) |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Target | Jointly learned VQ codes | $k$-means labels, refined offline | Frozen random codes | EMA-teacher latents |
| Target discrete? | Yes | Yes | Yes | **No** |
| Target moves during training? | Yes | Only between iterations | **Never** | Yes (slowly) |
| Loss | Contrastive (InfoNCE) | Cross-entropy | Cross-entropy | $L_2$ regression |
| Extra machinery | Gumbel-softmax, diversity loss | Clustering loop (multiple passes) | **None** | EMA teacher |
| Main failure mode | Codebook collapse | Poor initial units | Poor codebook luck (rare) | Teacher–student collapse |
| Scales cleanly? | Moderately | Awkward (clustering is a bottleneck) | **Yes** | Yes |

: Self-supervised objectives compared. {#tbl-ssl-families}

The trajectory across the table is toward *simplicity*: each family removes
machinery from the previous one while matching or beating it. That is usually a
sign that the field has identified which part of the original method was doing
the work — here, masked prediction against consistent categorical targets — and
is discarding the scaffolding that surrounded it.

**w2v-BERT** [@chung2021w2vbert] is the notable hybrid, combining a contrastive
module (whose job is to *learn* the discrete inventory) with a masked-LM module
(whose job is to model context over it) in a single end-to-end model. It is the
speech encoder of SeamlessM4T and, by inheritance, of a considerable amount of
multilingual speech infrastructure.


## What Do These Models Actually Learn? {#sec-layerwise}

This section contains the single most useful empirical fact in the chapter, and
it is the one that connects it to every other chapter in the book.

Self-supervised speech encoders are not uniform. Probing each Transformer layer
with a light classifier reveals a consistent **layer-wise division of labour**
[@pasad2021layerwise]:

| Depth | Information | Best downstream use |
|:------|:------------|:--------------------|
| Lowest layers (and the CNN front-end) | Local acoustics, channel, **speaker identity** | Speaker verification, diarization |
| Lower-middle | Phonetic categories, articulatory features | Phone recognition |
| Upper-middle | Word identity, lexical content | ASR |
| Top layers (large models) | **Reverts toward the pre-training target** | — often *worse* than the middle |

: Layer-wise organisation of self-supervised speech encoders. {#tbl-layerwise}

The last row is the counter-intuitive one and deserves an explanation. In large
wav2vec 2.0 models the topmost layers move measurably *back* toward the local,
quantised input features they were trained to predict, producing an
autoencoder-like curve in which representational quality for phonetic and
lexical content peaks in the middle of the network and then declines. The
practical implication is direct: **the final layer is usually the wrong choice**,
which is the opposite of the convention inherited from vision and text models.

Two further consequences run through this book:

- **ASR and speaker tasks want opposite ends of the same network.** Recognition
  benefits from suppressing speaker identity, so it draws on upper-middle
  layers; diarization and verification need speaker identity preserved, so they
  draw on the lowest layers (@sec-features). One encoder serves both only
  because it happens to keep the two kinds of information at different depths.
- **The standard remedy is to learn the mixture.** Rather than committing to a
  layer, downstream heads take a weighted sum over all $L{+}1$ layer outputs
  with learnable weights,

$$
\mathbf{h}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{L} w_l \, \mathbf{h}_t^{(l)},
\qquad \mathbf{w} = \operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})
$$ {#eq-layersum}

  where only $\boldsymbol{\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}^{L+1}$ is trained alongside the
  head. Inspecting the learned $\mathbf{w}$ afterwards is itself a diagnostic:
  the weight profile tells you where in the encoder your task's information
  lives.


## Evaluation: SUPERB and Its Discontents {#sec-superb}

Comparing self-supervised encoders is harder than comparing ASR systems, because
an encoder is not a system. Fine-tune it aggressively enough and any sufficiently
large model looks good, which measures the fine-tuning budget rather than the
representation.

**SUPERB** [@yang2021superb] resolved this with a protocol as important as its
leaderboard: **freeze the encoder, train only a lightweight task-specific head,
and use the learnable layer weighting of @eq-layersum.** Because the encoder
cannot adapt, the benchmark measures representation quality directly. The suite
spans ten tasks chosen to cover four distinct kinds of information:

| Category | Tasks |
|:---------|:------|
| Content | Phoneme Recognition, ASR, Keyword Spotting, Query-by-Example |
| Speaker | Speaker Identification, Automatic Speaker Verification, Speaker Diarization |
| Semantics | Intent Classification, Slot Filling |
| Paralinguistics | Emotion Recognition |

: The SUPERB task suite. {#tbl-superb}

That grouping is itself a claim worth noticing: it asserts that a good speech
representation must serve speaker, content, semantic, and paralinguistic
purposes simultaneously — which is precisely what @sec-layerwise says a single
encoder can only do by stratifying them across depth.

**ML-SUPERB** [@shi2023mlsuperb] extends the protocol to 143 languages with ASR
and language identification, and remains the main multilingual representation
benchmark.

**Known weaknesses**, which should be stated whenever SUPERB numbers are quoted:

- The frozen-encoder, light-head protocol does not necessarily predict
  performance under full fine-tuning, and almost certainly does not predict
  performance when the encoder is attached to an LLM decoder (@sec-llm-asr) —
  the dominant deployment pattern today.
- Scores are near-saturated on several tasks, so ranking differences are within
  noise.
- The head architecture and optimisation budget, though standardised, still
  advantage some representation geometries over others.


## Multilingual Scaling {#sec-multilingual}

Self-supervision's most consequential application is the long tail of languages.
Because pre-training needs no transcripts, a single model can absorb audio from
hundreds of languages at once and transfer to any of them.

| Model | Languages | Pre-training audio | Notes |
|:------|----------:|-------------------:|:------|
| XLSR / XLS-R [@babu2022xlsr] | 128 | 436k h | Established that one shared multilingual encoder beats per-language training, especially in the low-resource tail |
| MMS [@pratap2024mms] | 1,400+ | ~55k h labelled + unlabelled | ASR for 1,100+ languages; see the data caveat below |
| USM [@zhang2023usm] | 100–300+ | 12M h | BEST-RQ pre-training at industrial scale |
| XEUS [@chen2024xeus] | 4,000+ | ~1M h | Adds a dereverberation objective for robustness |

: Multilingual self-supervised speech models. {#tbl-multilingual}

The central empirical finding is **positive cross-lingual transfer**: a model
pre-trained on many languages outperforms a monolingual model on the *same*
low-resource target, because phonetic and articulatory structure is largely
shared even when lexicons are not. The effect is strongest exactly where it is
needed most, for languages with a few hours of data or fewer.

It is bounded, however, by the **curse of multilinguality**: at fixed capacity,
adding languages eventually degrades per-language quality, as the model trades
specialisation for coverage. This is the representation-learning counterpart of
the coverage tax measured on ASR leaderboards (@sec-leaderboard), and it is why
the largest multilingual models are also the largest models.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A data caveat worth teaching

MMS reached 1,000+ languages by using recordings of **religious texts** — chiefly
New Testament translations — because that is the only broadly parallel
multilingual speech corpus in existence. It is a genuinely clever piece of
data sourcing, and it also means the training distribution is a single register
(read, formal, liturgical), typically one or few speakers per language, with a
lexicon skewed toward a specific domain. Reported coverage of a language should
not be read as usable ASR for that language's everyday speech.
:::


## Foundation Encoders in Practice {#sec-foundation}

### Whisper as a Feature Extractor {#sec-whisper-encoder}

A pattern worth flagging because it now dominates deployment: the encoder from a
large *supervised* model is often used exactly as a self-supervised one would
be. Whisper's encoder (@sec-whisper), trained on 680k hours of weakly-labelled
data, produces representations that transfer well and are the input to a large
share of current audio language models, usually via a projector into an LLM's
embedding space.

The comparison to genuinely self-supervised encoders is instructive rather than
one-sided. Whisper's encoder is trained toward *transcription*, so it actively
suppresses information that is nuisance for that task — speaker identity,
emotion, background acoustics. This makes it an excellent front-end for
content-oriented tasks and a measurably poorer one for paralinguistic tasks, a
weakness that resurfaces in @sec-modality-gap as one mechanism behind audio
language models' difficulty with emotion and speaker attributes. WavLM remains
the better choice when the downstream task is about *who* is speaking or *how*
rather than *what*.

### Discrete Units as an Interface {#sec-discrete-units}

Running $k$-means over the middle layers of HuBERT or WavLM and keeping the
cluster indices yields a sequence of discrete symbols at roughly 50 Hz. These
are the **semantic tokens** referred to throughout the generative chapters of
this book. They capture phonetic and linguistic content while discarding speaker
identity and acoustic detail — which is to say, they are *not* invertible to
audio, and that is precisely why they are paired with acoustic tokens from a
neural codec in later architectures.

The interface matters more than any particular model: once speech is a sequence
of integers from a finite vocabulary, the entire language-modelling toolkit
applies unchanged. That observation is what the codec and speech-language-model
chapters are built on, and it originates here.

### Efficiency

Full-size encoders are expensive: wav2vec 2.0 Large and WavLM Large are around
300M parameters and were pre-trained on hundreds of GPU-days. Two responses are
standard. **Distillation** compresses a large encoder into a much smaller
student that retains most of the SUPERB performance — DistilHuBERT
[@chang2022distilhubert] predicts multiple teacher layers from a shared shallow
student, a design that follows directly from @sec-layerwise, since different
layers carry different information and must be preserved separately. **Partial
fine-tuning** freezes the encoder and trains only adapters or the layer weights
of @eq-layersum, which is often within noise of full fine-tuning at a fraction
of the cost.

### Toolkits

| Toolkit | Role | Repository |
|:--------|:-----|:-----------|
| **S3PRL** | Reference implementation of SUPERB; frozen-encoder benchmarking across many upstream models | [s3prl/s3prl](https://github.com/s3prl/s3prl) |
| **fairseq** | Original wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, data2vec, XLS-R, MMS implementations | [facebookresearch/fairseq](https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairseq) |
| **Transformers** | Inference and fine-tuning for most published encoders | [huggingface/transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers) |
| **SpeechBrain** | Recipes wrapping SSL encoders for downstream tasks | [speechbrain/speechbrain](https://github.com/speechbrain/speechbrain) |
| **ESPnet** | SSL front-ends inside full ASR/ST pipelines; XEUS | [espnet/espnet](https://github.com/espnet/espnet) |

: Toolkits for self-supervised speech representations. {#tbl-ssl-toolkits}

Extracting layer-wise features is a few lines:

```python
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoFeatureExtractor

name = "microsoft/wavlm-large"          # strongest general-purpose encoder
fe = AutoFeatureExtractor.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(name, output_hidden_states=True).eval()

inputs = fe(waveform, sampling_rate=16_000, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    hidden = model(**inputs).hidden_states   # tuple of (L+1) tensors

# Weighted layer sum; alpha is learned jointly with the downstream head
alpha = torch.zeros(len(hidden), requires_grad=True)
features = torch.einsum("l,lbtd->btd", alpha.softmax(0), torch.stack(hidden))
```


## Open Problems {#sec-ssl-open}

1. **What the units mean.** Discovered units correlate with phones but are not
   phones: they are context-dependent, split by speaker and channel, and vary in
   granularity with $k$. There is no principled account of what inventory a
   given objective and cluster count will produce, and no way to choose $k$
   other than by downstream trial.
2. **Scaling laws are poorly characterised.** For text, the relationship between
   compute, data, parameters, and loss is well mapped. For speech
   self-supervision it is not, and the pre-training loss is a weak predictor of
   downstream quality — a model with lower masked-prediction loss is not
   reliably a better encoder.
3. **The low-resource tail is still poor.** Coverage claims of 1,000+ languages
   are real, but quality at the tail is weak, the training data is often a
   single narrow register, and evaluation data barely exists — which means the
   tail is simultaneously the least good and the least measurable.
4. **Evaluation has outgrown SUPERB.** The frozen-encoder protocol was the right
   answer for 2021 and does not predict behaviour under the dominant current
   pattern of attaching an encoder to an LLM decoder. There is no widely
   accepted successor.
5. **Continuous or discrete?** This chapter's dominant recipe quantises the
   *target*, and downstream generative work quantises the *representation*. But
   data2vec works without quantisation, continuous features still beat discrete
   tokens on most discriminative downstream tasks, and the generative side has an
   active continuous-latent counter-movement. The question is genuinely open, and
   it recurs in @sec-continuous-alt.
6. **Robustness and fairness.** Encoders inherit the demographic and acoustic
   composition of their unlabelled pre-training data. Because that data is
   unlabelled, its composition is typically *unknown*, which makes the resulting
   biases harder to audit than the labelled-data disparities of
   @sec-asr-failures rather than easier.
7. **Paralinguistics are under-served.** Objectives reward predicting *what* was
   said. Prosody, emotion, and speaking style are largely incidental to that,
   and the resulting representational weakness propagates into every downstream
   paralinguistic task in this book.


## Summary

Self-supervised pre-training is the field's answer to the fact that unlabelled
speech outnumbers transcribed speech by orders of magnitude. The difficulty is
that speech is continuous and locally predictable, so a naive reconstruction
objective learns signal smoothness rather than linguistic structure. The
resolution the field converged on is **masked prediction against consistent
discrete targets**, and the three canonical objectives differ only in where
those targets come from: jointly-learned vector quantisation trained
contrastively (wav2vec 2.0), offline $k$-means labels refined by iterating the
model against its own representations (HuBERT, plus WavLM's denoising
augmentation), and a frozen random-projection codebook that is never learned at
all (BEST-RQ). The progression is toward removing machinery, which is the usual
signature of a field discovering which component was actually load-bearing.

The practical payoff is threefold. Usable ASR from minutes rather than thousands
of hours of labelled audio; a single encoder that transfers across hundreds of
languages through shared phonetic structure; and a general-purpose front-end
that serves speaker, content, and semantic tasks at once — though only because,
as @sec-layerwise shows, it stratifies those kinds of information across depth,
which is why the final layer is usually the wrong one to use and why ASR and
diarization draw from opposite ends of the same network.

Two threads leave this chapter for elsewhere in the book. Discrete units
obtained by clustering these encoders are the **semantic tokens** that the
codec and speech-language-model chapters depend on, and the pattern of
projecting a frozen encoder into a language model's embedding space —
whether that encoder is WavLM or Whisper's — is the architecture of essentially
every audio LLM.

The next chapter turns to the task that these representations were most
immediately useful for beyond recognition: determining not what was said, but
who said it, and when.
